name: Pomo, Eastern
confidence_why: McLendon's 1966 grammar of Eastern Pomo shows three phonemic stresses distinguishing word pairs, and her 1973 comparative study only adds that stress usually sits on the first or second syllable and always on the root in verbs while staying unpredictable in nouns, so the fixed: initial syllable coding in Gordon 2002 is outweighed by the describer herself, though the whole record rests on one fieldworker.

It is primarily a pitch accent (tone) in Pn and stress in Pc, Pne, and Pe. In Pe its location is partially predictable morphologically: stress always occurs on the root in verbs. There is, however, no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns. [preceded by:] Synchronically, the seven Pomo daughter languages have the following prosodic systems. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (src gordon) records fixed initial stress (initial stress). McLendon 1973 instead describes a phonemic accent occurring 'mostly on the first or second syllable', morphologically bound to the root in verbs and unpredictable in most nouns — a lexical/morphological system, not a fixed: initial syllable one. The only Pomoan language McLendon says has fixed initial stress is Southeastern Pomo (Pse), not Eastern Pomo. Caveat: the item is a lending-library copy (access-restricted; could not be reached by automated download then 403), so the reading rests on overlapping full-text-search highlight fragments stitched together, not on a continuous page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Eastern Pomo (Pe) has a phonemic (contrastive) stress accent that falls mostly on the first or second syllable of the word; in verbs it is fixed on the root syllable, so its position is morphologically predictable there; in most nouns there is no synchronic way to identify a root, so noun stress is effectively lexical. McLendon also reconstructs a phonemic pitch-stress accent for Proto Pomo that was 'probably morphologically predictable — presumably occurring on the root syllable', and notes that certain affixes 'have their own accent, which then suppresses that normally occurring on the root'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any fragment recovered.
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns: 'no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns' (the sentence continues 'Halpern (MS) suggests that the same pattern..', cut off by the fragment window). Affixes carrying their own accent suppress the root accent (§134 fragment). The accent is described as 'mostly' on syllable 1 or 2, i.e. not exceptionless.
new_statements.identity_note: McLendon's 'Pe' is Eastern Pomo proper (her own fieldwork language; the book's informant table lists Pe under McLendon). The statement is a synchronic summary inside a comparative reconstruction of Proto Pomo, not a dialect-specific description; no particular Eastern Pomo dialect (Big Valley vs Upper Lake) is named in the recovered fragments.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (src gordon) carries the fixed: initial syllable pattern string initial stress. McLendon 1973 (1971 typescript) instead states a phonemic stress accent on the first OR second syllable, root-bound in verbs and lexical in nouns: not fixed initial (fixed initial stress is what she reports for Southeastern Pomo, Pse). It AGREES with the existing_statement held by the project (same work, same passage, reading 'morphologically determined', now confirmed from a continuous page rather than stitched snippets) and is consistent with the catalog_quote from McLendon 1966 sec. 130-131 (three phonemic stresses with minimal pairs /xa·máwi·nà·/ vs /xa·màwi·ná·/).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Eastern Pomo (Pe) has a phonemic (contrastive) STRESS accent, realized as stress (not pitch), falling mostly on the first or second syllable of the word; in verbs stress always falls on the root, so its position is morphologically predictable there; in most nouns roots cannot be identified synchronically, so accent position is lexically specified. Diachronically (sec. 135) Pe kept the Proto-Pomo phonemic accent and deleted pre-tonic syllables beginning with *ʔ or *h, turning many proto second-syllable accents into initial accents. The only Pomoan language the work describes with fixed initial stress is Southeastern Pomo (Pse); Southern Pomo (Ps) has penult stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in Eastern Pomo; a 'secondary accent' is mentioned only for the Proto-Pomo reconstruction of two old compounds (ASHES, TEARS), typescript p. 37 = p. 53. (McLendon 1966 sec. 130, already held by the project, gives Pe three phonemic stress degrees.)
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns: 'no synchronic basis for identifying roots in most nouns' (accent position not predictable there); Halpern (ms.) is cited for the same partial morphological predictability in Pn, Pc and Pne; accent 'mostly' (not always) on the first or second syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Eastern Pomo (Pe, Clear Lake, California), one of the seven Pomoan daughter languages compared in the work (Pk Kashaya, Ps Southern, Pc Central, Pn Northern, Pne Northeastern, Pe Eastern, Pse Southeastern); McLendon's Pe data are her own field data (the language of her 1966 dissertation / 1975 grammar).

readall_conflicts: One disagreement: the catalog's gordon record gives Eastern Pomo fixed initial stress, whereas McLendon 1973 (§135, p. 34) says Eastern Pomo has a phonemic accent 'mostly on the first or second syllable', fixed on the root in verbs and with no synchronic root to anchor it in most nouns. That is a type difference (lexical/morphological vs fixed: initial syllable), not merely a placement detail. McLendon's own within-family statements (Southeastern Pomo always initial; Southern Pomo penultimate per Halpern; Northern Pomo pitch accent) are about other Pomoan languages and do not bear on the Eastern Pomo entry. No other work was listed for this item. McLendon 1973 (read here from the open 1971 typescript, sec. 130, typescript p. 36) contradicts the catalog's fixed: initial syllable pattern string (initial stress, src gordon) for Eastern Pomo: she describes a phonemic stress accent falling on the first or second syllable, always on the root in verbs and lexically placed in nouns, and reserves fixed initial stress for Southeastern Pomo. The work agrees with the existing statement held by the project drawn from the same passage (previously stitched from archive.org search snippets, now confirmed on a continuous page scan) and with McLendon 1966 sec. 130-131 (three contrastive stress degrees with minimal pairs) quoted in the catalog. No disagreement among the McLendon sources themselves; the disagreement is between them and the gordon-derived fixed: initial syllable coding.
